'''Agroforestry''' (also known as '''agro-sylviculture''' or '''forest farming''') is a [[land use]] management system that integrates [[tree]]s with [[crop]]s or [[pasture]]. It combines [[agricultural]] and [[forestry]] technologies. As a [[polyculture]] system, an agroforestry system can produce timber and [[wood]] products, [[fruit]]s, [[Nut (fruit)|nut]]s, other [[edible plant]] products, [[edible mushroom]]s, [[medicinal plant]]s, [[ornamental plant]]s, animals and [[animal product]]s, and other products from both domesticated and wild species.<ref name=":2">{{cite book |last1=Mudge |first1=Ken |last2=Gabriel |first2=Steve |title=Farming the Woods: an integrated permaculture approach to growing food and medicinals in temperate forests |date=2014 |publisher=[[Chelsea Green Publishing]] |location=White River Junction, VT| page=9|isbn=978-1-60358-507-1}}</ref>

Agroforestry can be practiced for economic, environmental, and social benefits, and can be part of [[Sustainability|sustainable]] agriculture.<ref name="aftaweb">{{Cite web |title=What is agroforestry? |url=http://www.aftaweb.org/about/what-is-agroforestry.html |access-date=2018-04-29 |website=aftaweb.org}}</ref> Apart from production, benefits from agroforestry include improved farm productivity,<ref>{{Cite journal |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sd.2956|title=Fostering sustainable production via the Amazon Fund collaborative platform |first1=Eduardo |last1=Bizzo |first2=Gregory |last2=Michener |date=March 17, 2024 |journal=Sustainable Development |volume=32 |issue=5 |pages=5129–5143 |via=CrossRef |doi=10.1002/sd.2956 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> healthier environments, reduction of risk for farmers,<ref>{{cite book |last1=MacDicken |first1=Kenneth G. |last2=Vergara |first2=Napoleon T. |title=Agroforestry: classification and management |date=1990 |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|John Wiley & Sons]] |isbn=0-471-83781-4 |page=2}}</ref> beauty and aesthetics, increased farm profits, reduced soil erosion, creating wildlife habitat, less pollution, managing animal waste, increased biodiversity, improved soil structure, and [[carbon sequestration]].

Agroforestry practices are especially prevalent in the tropics, especially in subsistence [[smallholding]]s areas, with particular importance in sub-Saharan Africa. Due to its multiple benefits, for instance in [[nutrient cycle]] benefits and potential for mitigating droughts, it has been adopted in the US and Europe.<ref>{{Citation |last=Franzel |first=Steven |title=Valuing Agroforestry Systems |chapter=Financial Analysis of Agroforestry Practices |series=Advances in Agroforestry |date=2005 |volume=2 |pages=9–37 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/1-4020-2413-4_2 |access-date=2026-03-04 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Kluwer Academic Publishers |doi=10.1007/1-4020-2413-4_2 |isbn=1-4020-2412-6}}</ref>

== Definition ==

At its most basic, agroforestry is any of various [[polyculture]] systems that intentionally integrate [[tree]]s with [[crop]]s or [[pasture]] on the same land.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Agroforestry |url=https://www.fao.org/forestry/agroforestry/80338/en/ |access-date=2022-02-26 |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization]] |archive-date=4 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221104071119/https://www.fao.org/forestry/agroforestry/80338/en/}}</ref><ref name="aftaweb"/><ref>Leakey, R.R.B. (1996). Definition of agroforestry revisited, Agroforestry Today, 8(1), 5-7.</ref> An agroforestry system is intensively managed to optimize helpful interactions between the plants and animals included, and "uses the forest as a model of practices".<ref name=":2" /> The integration of tree species into farming systems initiates the development of an agroecological succession akin to natural vegetation. Hence, agroforestry is applied agroecology.<ref>Leakey, R.R.B. 2014. The role of trees in agroecology and sustainable agriculture in the tropics. Annual Review of Phytopathology 52: 113-133.</ref>

Agroforestry shares principles with polyculture practices such as [[intercropping]], but can also involve much more complex multi-strata agroforests containing hundreds of species. Agroforestry can also utilise [[Nitrogen fixation#Biological|nitrogen-fixing plants]] such as [[legumes]] to restore soil nitrogen fertility. Many farmers practicing agroforestry do not identify their land use as "agroforestry", signaling a need for greater education and awareness to increase adoption of these sustainable practices.<ref>Santiago-Freijanes et al. 2021; Mosquera-Losada et al. 2020.</ref>

== History and scientific study ==

The term "agroforestry" was coined in 1973 by Canadian forester John Bene, but the concept includes agricultural practices that have existed for millennia.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mudge |first1=Ken |last2=Gabriel |first2=Steve |title=Farming the Woods: an integrated permaculture approach to growing food and medicinals in temperate forests |date=2014 |publisher=[[Chelsea Green Publishing]] |page=2 |isbn=978-1-60358-507-1}}</ref>
Scientific agroforestry began in the 20th century with [[Ethnobotany|ethnobotanical]] studies carried out by [[Anthropology|anthropologists]]. However, indigenous communities that have lived in close relationships with [[Forest ecology|forest ecosystems]] have practiced agroforestry informally for centuries.<ref name="bhasakar"/> For example, [[Indigenous peoples of California]] periodically burned oak and other habitats to maintain a 'pyrodiversity collecting model,' which allowed for improved tree health and habitat conditions.<ref>{{cite book |last=Lightfoot |first=Kent |title=California Indians and Their Environment: An Introduction |year=2009 |location=Berkeley |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |url={{google books |plainurl=y |id=bdAKPOEfrooC}}}}</ref> Likewise Native Americans in the eastern United States extensively altered their environment and managed land as a "mosaic" of woodland areas, [[orchard]]s, and forest gardens.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mudge |first1=Ken |last2=Gabriel |first2=Steve |title=Farming the Woods: an integrated permaculture approach to growing food and medicinals in temperate forests |date=2014 |publisher=[[Chelsea Green Publishing]] | page=23|isbn=978-1-60358-507-1}}</ref>

Agroforestry in the [[tropics]] is ancient and widespread, notably in the form of "tropical home gardens." Some of those plots have been continuously cultivated for centuries. A "home garden" in Central America could contain 25 different species of trees and food crops on just one-tenth of an acre.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mudge |first1=Ken |last2=Gabriel |first2=Steve |title=Farming the Woods: an integrated permaculture approach to growing food and medicinals in temperate forests |date=2014 |publisher=Chelsea Green Publishing |pages=38–39 |isbn=978-1-60358-507-1}}</ref> "Tropical home gardens" are traditional systems developed over time by growers without formalized research or institutional support, and are characterized by a high complexity and diversity of useful plants, with a canopy of tree and palm species that produce food, fuel, and shade, a mid-story of shrubs for fruit or spices, and an understory of root vegetables, medicinal herbs, beans, ornamental plants, and other non-woody crops.<ref>{{cite book |last1=MacDicken |first1=Kenneth G. |last2=Vergara |first2=Napoleon T. |title=Agroforestry: classification and management |date=1990 |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|John Wiley & Sons]] |isbn=0-471-83781-4 |page=103}}</ref>

In 1929, J. Russel Smith published ''Tree Crops: A Permanent Agriculture'', in which he argued that American agriculture should be changed two ways: by using non-arable land for tree agriculture, and by using tree-produced crops to replace the grain inputs in the diets of livestock. Smith wrote that the [[Gleditsia triacanthos|honey locust]] tree, a legume that produced pods that could be used as nutritious livestock feed, had great potential as a crop. The book's subtitle later led to the coining of the term ''[[permaculture]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mudge |first1=Ken |last2=Gabriel |first2=Steve |title=Farming the Woods: an integrated permaculture approach to growing food and medicinals in temperate forests |date=2014 |publisher=[[Chelsea Green Publishing]] |pages=29–31|isbn=978-1-60358-507-1}}</ref>

The most studied agroforestry practices involve a simple interaction between two components, such as simple configurations of hedges or trees integrated with a single crop.<ref name=":10">{{cite journal |last1=Castle |first1=Sarah E. |last2=Miller |first2=Daniel C |last3=Merten |first3=Nikolas |last4=Ordonez |first4=Pablo J. |last5=Baylis |first5=Kathy |title=Evidence for the impacts of agroforestry on ecosystem services and human well-being in high-income countries: a systematic map |journal=Environmental Evidence |year=2022 |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=10 |doi=10.1186/s13750-022-00260-4 |s2cid=247501751 |doi-access=free |pmid=39294716 |bibcode=2022EnvEv..11...10C |pmc=11378871}}</ref> There is significant variation in agroforestry systems and the benefits they have.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=Sarah Jane |last2=Schelhas |first2=John |last3=Grau |first3=Ricardo |last4=Nanni |first4=A Sofia |last5=Sloan |first5=Sean |title=Forest ecosystem-service transitions: the ecological dimensions of the forest transition |journal=[[Ecology and Society]] |year=2017 |volume=22 |issue=4 |article-number=art38 |doi=10.5751/ES-09615-220438 |bibcode=2017EcSoc..22Tr.38W |hdl=11336/67453 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> Agroforestry as understood by modern science is derived from traditional indigenous and local practices, developed by living in close association with ecosystems for many generations.<ref name="bhasakar">{{cite book |last1=Vira |first1=Bhasakar |last2=Wildburger |first2=Christoph |last3=Mansourian |first3=Stephanie |title=Forests and Food: Addressing Hunger and Nutrition Across Sustainable Landscapes |date=2015 |publisher=Open Book Publishers |pages=73–136}}</ref>

Ninety-one countries and areas reported a total land area subject to agroforestry of 55.4 million hectares in 2025. The majority (39.3 million ha) of this area is in Asia, mostly South and Southeast Asia, with India and Indonesia accounting for almost 100% of the regional total and for 70% of the global total.<ref>{{Cite book |last=FAO |url=https://openknowledge.fao.org/handle/20.500.14283/cd6709en |title=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025 |date=2025 |publisher=FAO |isbn=978-92-5-140082-1 |language=English |doi=10.4060/cd6709en}}</ref>

== Benefits ==

Benefits include increasing farm productivity and profitability, reduced soil erosion, creating wildlife habitat, managing animal waste,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Agroforestry- A Sustainable Solution to Address Climate Change Challenges |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/313011619 |access-date=2021-07-23 |website=ResearchGate}}</ref> increased biodiversity, improved soil structure, and [[carbon sequestration]].<ref name="USDA">{{cite web |title=National Agroforestry Center |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/nac/practices/index.shtml |publisher=[[USDA]] National Agroforestry Center}}</ref>

Agroforestry systems can provide advantages over conventional agricultural and forest production methods. They can offer increased productivity; social, economic and environmental benefits, as well as greater diversity in the ecological goods and services provided.<ref name="Benefits of agroforestry">{{cite web |url=https://www.agroforestry.co.uk/about-agroforestry |title=Benefits of agroforestry |publisher=Agroforestry Research Trust [in England] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150420201730/http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/afbens.html |archive-date=20 April 2015}}</ref> These benefits are conditional on good farm management. This includes choosing the right trees, as well as pruning them regularly etc.<ref name="ta">{{cite journal |last1=Kuyah |first1=Shem |last2=Öborn |first2=Ingrid |last3=Jonsson |first3=Mattias |last4=Dahlin |first4=A Sigrun |last5=Barrios |first5=Edmundo |last6=Muthuri |first6=Catherine |last7=Malmer |first7=Anders |last8=Nyaga |first8=John |last9=Magaju |first9=Christine |last10=Namirembe |first10=Sara |last11=Nyberg |first11=Ylva |last12=Sinclair |first12=Fergus L. |display-authors=5 |title=Trees in agricultural landscapes enhance provision of ecosystem services in Sub-Saharan Africa |journal=International Journal of Biodiversity Science, Ecosystem Services & Management |date=2016-07-31 |volume=12 |issue=4 |page=255 |doi=10.1080/21513732.2016.1214178 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2016IJBSE..12..255K }}</ref>

=== Biodiversity ===

Agroforestry supports [[biodiversity]] in different ways. It provides a more diverse habitat than a conventional agricultural system in which the tree component creates ecological niches for a wide range of organisms both above and below ground. The life cycles and food chains associated with this diversification initiate an agroecological succession that creates functional [[agroecosystem]]s that confer sustainability. Tropical bat and bird diversity, for instance, can be comparable to the diversity in natural forests.<ref name="Harvey et. al, 2007">{{Cite journal |last1=Harvey |first1=Celia A. |last2=Villalobos |first2=Jorge A. González |date=1 July 2007 |title=Agroforestry systems conserve species-rich but modified assemblages of tropical birds and bats |journal=[[Biodiversity and Conservation]] |volume=16 |issue=8 |pages=2257–2292 |doi=10.1007/s10531-007-9194-2 |bibcode=2007BiCon..16.2257H |hdl=11056/22760 |s2cid=8412676 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> Although agroforestry systems do not provide as many floristic species as forests and do not show the same canopy height, they do provide food and nesting possibilities. A further contribution to biodiversity is that the [[germplasm]] of sensitive species can be preserved.<ref name="Jose, 2009">Jose, S. (2009). Agroforestry for [[ecosystem services]] and environmental benefits: an overview. Agroforestry Systems, 76(1), 1–10. {{doi |10.1007/s10457-009-9229-7}}</ref> As agroforests have no natural clear areas, habitats are more uniform. Furthermore, agroforests can serve as corridors between habitats. Agroforestry can help conserve biodiversity, positively influencing other ecosystem services.<ref name="Jose, 2009"/>

=== Soil and plant growth ===

Depleted soil can be protected from [[soil erosion]] by [[groundcover]] plants such as naturally growing grasses in agroforestry systems. These help to stabilise the soil as they increase cover compared to short-cycle cropping systems.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Nair |first1=P. K. Ramachandran |chapter=Soils and Agroforestry: General Principles |date=2021 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-030-75358-0_15 |title=An Introduction to Agroforestry |pages=367–382 |access-date=2023-05-13 |place=Cham |publisher=[[Springer International Publishing]] |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-75358-0_15 |isbn=978-3-030-75357-3 |last2=Kumar |first2=B. === Sustainability ===

Agroforestry systems can provide ecosystem services which can contribute to [[sustainable agriculture]] in the following ways:

* Diversification of agricultural products, such as fuelwood, medicinal plants, and multiple crops, increases income security<ref name="cr">Reij, C. and R. Winterbottom (2015). Scaling up Regreening: Six Steps to Success. World Resources Institute, World Resources Institute: 1-72.</ref>
* Increased [[food security]] and [[nutrition]] by restored [[soil fertility]], crop diversity and resilience to weather shocks for food crops<ref name="cr"/>
*Land restoration through reducing soil erosion and regulating water availability<ref name="lr"/>
* Possibility of reduced chemicals inputs, e.g. due to improved use of [[fertilizer]], increased resilience against [[Pest (organism)|pests]],<ref name="ta"/> and increased ground cover which reduces weeds<ref name="Nchanji Nkonghu 2016">{{cite journal |last1=Nchanji |first1=Yvonne K. |last2=Nkongho |first2=Raymond N. |last3=Mala |first3=William A. |last4=Levang |first4=Patrice |title=Efficacy of oil palm intercropping by smallholders. Case study in South-West Cameroon |journal=Agroforestry Systems |volume=90 |issue=3 |year=2016 |doi=10.1007/s10457-015-9873-z |pages=509–519 |bibcode=2016AgrSy..90..509N |doi-access=free |hdl=10568/94989 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

According to the [[Food and Agriculture Organization]]'s ''The State of the World's Forests 2020'', adopting agroforestry and sustainable production practices, restoring the productivity of degraded agricultural lands, embracing healthier diets and reducing food loss and waste are all actions that urgently need to be scaled up. Agribusinesses must meet their commitments to deforestation-free commodity chains and companies that have not made zero-deforestation commitments should do so.<ref>{{cite book |title=The State of the World's Forests 2020. Forests, biodiversity and people – In brief |publisher=[[FAO]] & [[UNEP]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-92-5-132707-4 |location=Rome |doi=10.4060/ca8985en |s2cid=241416114}}</ref>

=== Other environmental goals ===

[[Carbon sequestration]] is an important ecosystem service.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kay |first1=Sonja |last2=Rega |first2=Carlo |last3=Moreno |first3=Gerardo |last4=den Herder |first4=Michael |last5=Palma |first5=João H.N. |last6=Borek |first6=Robert |last7=Crous-Duran |first7=Josep |last8=Freese |first8=Dirk |last9=Giannitsopoulos |first9=Michail |last10=Graves |first10=Anil |last11=Jäger |first11=Mareike |last12=Lamersdorf |first12=Norbert |last13=Memedemin |first13=Daniyar |last14=Mosquera-Losada |first14=Rosa |last15=Pantera |first15=Anastasia |display-authors=5 |date=April 2019 |title=Agroforestry creates carbon sinks whilst enhancing the environment in agricultural landscapes in Europe |journal=Land Use Policy |volume=83 |pages=581–593 |doi=10.1016/j.landusepol.2019.02.025 |s2cid=159179077 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019LUPol..83..581K |hdl=10347/22156 |hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Jose, 2009"/><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-02-07 |title=Multistrata Agroforestry |url=https://drawdown.org/solutions/multistrata-agroforestry |access-date=2020-12-04 |website=Project Drawdown}}</ref> Agroforestry practices can increase carbon stocks in soil and woody biomass.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.nap.edu/read/25259/chapter/5 |title=Read "Negative Emissions Technologies and Reliable Sequestration: A Research Agenda" at NAP.edu |year=2019 |doi=10.17226/25259 |pmid=31120708 |isbn=978-0-309-48452-7 |s2cid=134196575 |language=en}}</ref> Trees in agroforestry systems, like in new forests, can recapture some of the carbon that was lost by cutting existing forests. They also provide additional food and products. The rotation age and the use of the resulting products are important factors controlling the amount of carbon sequestered. Agroforests can reduce pressure on primary forests by providing forest products.<ref name="Montagnini et. al., 2004">{{Cite journal |last1=Montagnini |first1=F. |last2=Nair |first2=P. K. R. |date=1 July 2004 |title=Carbon sequestration: An underexploited environmental benefit of agroforestry systems |journal=Agroforestry Systems |volume=61–62 |issue=1–3 |page=281 |doi=10.1023/B:AGFO.0000029005.92691.79 |bibcode=2004AgrSy..61..281M |s2cid=33847583}}</ref>

=== Adaptation to climate change ===

Agroforestry can significantly contribute to [[climate change mitigation]] along with adaptation benefits.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zomer |first1=Robert J. |last2=Neufeldt |first2=Henry |last3=Xu |first3=Jianchu |last4=Ahrends |first4=Antje |last5=Bossio |first5=Deborah |last6=Trabucco |first6=Antonio |last7=van Noordwijk |first7=Meine |last8=Wang |first8=Mingcheng |display-authors=5 |date=20 July 2016 |title=Global Tree Cover and Biomass Carbon on Agricultural Land: The contribution of agroforestry to global and national carbon budgets |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=6 |issue=1 |article-number=29987 |doi=10.1038/srep29987 |pmid=27435095 |pmc=4951720 |bibcode=2016NatSR...629987Z |doi-access=free}}</ref> A case study in Kenya found that the adoption of agroforestry drove carbon storage and increased livelihoods simultaneously among small-scale farmers. In this case, maintaining the diversity of tree species, especially land use and farm size are important factors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Reppin |first1=Saskia |last2=Kuyah |first2=Shem |last3=de Neergaard |first3=Andreas |last4=Oelofse |first4=Myles |last5=Rosenstock |first5=Todd S. |date=16 March 2019 |title=Contribution of agroforestry to climate change mitigation and livelihoods in Western Kenya |journal=Agroforestry Systems |volume=94 |pages=203–220 |doi=10.1007/s10457-019-00383-7 |doi-access=free|hdl=10568/106005 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Poor smallholder farmers have turned to agroforestry as a means to adapt to [[climate change]]. A study from the [[CGIAR]] research program on Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security found from a survey of over 700 households in East Africa that at least 50% of those households had begun planting trees in a change from earlier practices. The trees were planted with fruit, tea, coffee, oil, fodder and medicinal products in addition to their usual harvest. Agroforestry was one of the most widespread adaptation strategies, along with the use of improved crop varieties and intercropping.<ref name="Kristjanson et al">{{cite journal |last1=Kristjanson |first1=Patti |last2=Neufeldt |first2=Henry |last3=Gassner |first3=Anja |last4=Mango |first4=Joash |last5=Kyazze |first5=Florence B. |last6=Desta |first6=Solomon |last7=Sayula |first7=George |last8=Thiede |first8=Brian |last9=Förch |first9=Wiebke |last10=Thornton |first10=Philip K. |last11=Coe |first11=Richard |display-authors=5 |title=Are food insecure smallholder households making changes in their farming practices? Evidence from East Africa |journal=Food Security |volume=4 |issue=3 |year=2012 |doi=10.1007/s12571-012-0194-z |pages=381–397|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Tropical ==

{{see also|Applications of agroforestry}}

''Kuojtakiloyan'' is a [[Sierra Puebla Nahuatl|Masehual]] term that means 'useful forest' or 'forest that produces', and it is an agroforestry system developed and maintained by indigenous peoples of the [[Sierra Norte de Puebla|Sierra Norte]] of the [[Puebla|State of Puebla]], [[Mexico]]. It has become a vital fountain of resources (food, medicinal herbs, fuels, [[floriculture]], etc.) for the local population, but it is also a respectful transformation of the environment, with its [[biodiversity]] and [[nature conservation]]. The ''kuojtakiloyan'' comes directly from the ancestral [[Nahuas|Nahua]] and [[Totonac|Totonaku]] knowledge of their natural environment.<ref name="lm">{{Cite news |last=Toledo |first=V. The ''kuojtakiloyan'' is a jungle-landscaped [[polyculture]] in which [[avocado]]s, [[sweet potatoes]], [[cinnamon]], [[Prunus salicifolia|black cherries]], [[Inga|chalahuits]], [[citrus fruits]], [[gourd]]s, [[macadamia]], [[mango]]es, [[banana]]s and [[sapote]]s are grown.<ref name="lm"/><ref name="Moreno-Calles 2013" /> In addition, a wide variety of harvested wild edible mushrooms and herbs (''[[quelite (disambiguation)|quelites]]''). === Alley cropping ===

{{main|Alley cropping}}

With alley cropping, crop strips alternate with rows of closely spaced tree or hedge species. Normally, the trees are pruned before planting the crop. The cut leafy material - for example, from ''[[Alchornea cordifolia]]'' and ''[[Acioa barteri]]'' - is spread over the crop area to provide nutrients. The hedges serve as windbreaks and reduce erosion.<ref name="Tripathi-Psychas-1992"/> In tropical areas of North and South America, various species of ''[[Inga]]'' such as ''[[Inga edulis|I. edulis]]'' and ''[[Inga oerstediana|I. oerstediana]]'' have been used for alley cropping.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://theecologist.org/2005/feb/20/rainforest-saver |title=The Rainforest Saver |work=The Ecologist |first=Daniel |last=Elkan |date=20 February 2005}}</ref> [[Weed control]] is inherent to the practice, providing mulch and shade.<ref name="Tripathi-Psychas-1992">{{cite book |last1=Tripathi |first1=Bansh R. |last2=Psychas |first2=Paul J. |title=The AFNETA Alley Farming Training Manual |publisher=[[Alley Farming Network for Tropical Africa]] (AFNETA) |date=1992 |hdl=10568/49807 |volume=1 - Core course in alley farming |isbn=978-131-074-X |oclc=29771935 |publication-place=[[Ibadan]] |pages=xi+180 |s2cid=130266228}} [[AGRIS]] id [http://agris.fao.org/agris-search/search.do?recordID=XF2016015795 XF2016015795]. {{hdl |20.500.12478/5101}}.</ref>

The [[United States Department of Agriculture]] distinguishes five applications of agroforestry for [[temperate climates]], namely alley cropping, forest farming, riparian forest buffers, silvopasture, and windbreaks.<ref name="USDA"/>

=== Alley cropping ===<!--USDA application #1 -->

Alley cropping can also be used in temperate climates. Strip cropping is similar to alley cropping in that trees alternate with crops. The difference is that, with alley cropping, the trees are in single rows. With strip cropping, the trees or shrubs are planted in wide strips. The purpose can be, as with alley cropping, to provide nutrients, in leaf form, to the crop. With strip cropping, the trees can have a purely productive role, providing fruits, nuts, etc. while, at the same time, protecting nearby crops from soil erosion and harmful winds.<ref name="USDA"/>

=== Forest farming ===<!--USDA application #2 -->

In forest farming, high-value crops are grown under a suitably-managed tree canopy. This is sometimes called multi-story cropping, or in tropical villages as home gardening. It can be practised at varying levels of intensity but always involves some degree of management; this distinguishes it from simple harvesting of wild plants from the forest.<ref name="USDA"/><!--https://www.fs.usda.gov/nac/practices/forest-farming.php-->

=== Riparian forest buffers ===<!--USDA application #3 -->

[[File:Riparian buffer on Bear Creek in Story County, Iowa.JPG|thumb |upright |A [[riparian buffer]] bordering a river in Iowa]]

[[Riparian buffer]]s are strips of permanent vegetation located along or near active watercourses or in ditches where [[surface runoff|water runoff]] concentrates. The purpose is to keep nutrients and soil from contaminating the water.<ref name="USDA"/>

=== Silvopasture ===<!--USDA application #4 -->

[[File:Agrosylviculture australie Clive Wawn.jpg|thumb|Silvopasture over the years (Australia)]]

Trees can benefit fauna in a [[silvopasture]] system, where cattle, goats, or sheep browse on grasses grown under trees.<ref name="USDA"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.agroforestry.co.uk/about-agroforestry/silvopasture/ |title=Silvopasture |publisher=Agroforestry Research Trust [in England] |access-date=19 August 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150420215242/http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/silvop.html |archive-date=20 April 2015}}</ref>

The ''[[dehesa]]'' or ''montado'' system of [[silviculture]] are an example of pigs and bulls being held [[extensive farming|extensively]] in Spain and [[Portugal]].<ref>Fra. Paleo, Urbano. (2010). "The dehesa/montado landscape". pp. 149–151 in Sustainable Use of Biological Diversity in Socio-ecological Production Landscapes, eds. Bélair, C., Ichikawa, K., Wong, B.Y.L. and Mulongoy, K.J. Montreal: Secretariat of the [[Convention on Biological Diversity]]. Technical Series no. 52.</ref>

=== Windbreaks ===<!--USDA application #5 -->

[[Windbreaks]] reduce wind velocity over and around crops. This increases yields through reduced drying of the crop and/or by preventing the crop from toppling in strong wind gusts.<ref name="USDA"/>

== Urban ==

'''Urban agroforestry''' is the application of agroforestry principles in urban and suburban environments, where reduced ecological functioning is common. It involves the deliberate integration of trees with shrubs and crops, which together ultimately produce an agricultural product, into managed landscapes such as residential backyards, public parks, and streetscapes.<ref name="pi">{{Cite journal |last=Lovell |first=Sarah |date=2020-05-19 |title=Urban agroforestry and its potential integration into city planning efforts |journal=Urban Agriculture & Regional Food Systems |language=en |volume=5 |issue=1 |article-number=e20000 |doi=10.1002/uar2.20000 |issn=2575-1220|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Benefits ===
The [[United Nations|UN]] state that the implementation of urban agroforestry systems offer a range of ecosystem services that can improve the health and resilience of urban areas. These benefits include improving [[Climate resilience|environmental resilience]], biodiversity, and social and cultural wellbeing.<ref name="wm">{{Cite web |title=The Edible City: Why Food Trees Matter |url=https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/2422244_E_PDF_WEB_0.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250219135632/https://unece.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/2422244_E_PDF_WEB_0.pdf |archive-date=2025-02-19 |website=unece.org |access-date=2026-03-04}}</ref>

==== Environmental resilience ====
The integration of agroforestry systems into rooftop gardens improves insulation of buildings reducing the demand of energy for cooling by up to 20%.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ASHRAE European Policy Update – May 15, 2025 – ASHRAE |url=https://ashrae-ireland.org/2025/05/15/ashrae-european-policy-update-may-15-2025/ |access-date=2026-01-29 |language=en-US}}</ref> Moreover, agroforestry systems increase permeable surfaces that alleviate urban drainage systems and enhance [[stormwater]] management.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Do Trees Improve Air Quality? – The Institute for Environmental Research and Education |date=4 June 2025 |url=https://iere.org/how-do-trees-improve-air-quality/ |access-date=2026-01-29 |language=en-US}}</ref> Finally, agroforestry systems improve air quality by absorbing pollutants like [[nitrogen dioxide]], [[ozone]] and [[particulate matter]], as well as releasing [[oxygen]] as quantified by several studies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alam |first1=Mahbubul |last2=Olivier |first2=Alain |last3=Paquette |first3=Alain |last4=Dupras |first4=Jérôme |last5=Revéret |first5=Jean-Pierre |last6=Messier |first6=Christian |date=2014-08-01 |title=A general framework for the quantification and valuation of ecosystem services of tree-based intercropping systems |journal=Agroforestry Systems |language=en |volume=88 |issue=4 |pages=679–691 |doi=10.1007/s10457-014-9681-x |bibcode=2014AgrSy..88..679A |issn=1572-9680}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stewart |first1=Stephen |last2=O'Grady |first2=Anthony |last3=Mendham |first3=Daniel |last4=Smith |first4=Greg |last5=Smethurst |first5=Philip |date=2022-09-27 |title=Digital Tools for Quantifying the Natural Capital Benefits of Agroforestry: A Review |journal=Land |language=en |volume=11 |issue=10 |page=1668 |doi=10.3390/land11101668 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2022Land...11.1668S |issn=2073-445X}}</ref><ref name=":10" />

==== Biodiversity ====
The incorporation of a vast variety of trees, shrubs, and crops creates heterogeneous habitats for various species such as pollinators, birds and small mammals leading to an increase in biodiversity. In addition, through an enhanced connectivity between habitats the persistent problem of [[habitat fragmentation]] in urban areas is alleviated.<ref name="wm"/> However, the current evidence base remains limited, with studies focusing mostly on the improvement of avian diversity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Exantus |first1=Jean-Marry |last2=Beaune |first2=David |last3=Cézilly |first3=Frank |date=2021-08-01 |title=The relevance of urban agroforestry and urban remnant forest for avian diversity in a densely-populated developing country: The case of Port-au-Prince, Haiti |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |volume=63 |article-number=127217 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2021.127217 |issn=1618-8667|doi-access=free |bibcode=2021UFUG...6327217E }}</ref> Overall, the literature supports a context-dependent benefit of agroforestry systems for biodiversity, while indicating the need for further research across a broader range of taxonomic groups, focussing more on urban and suburban areas.

==== Social and cultural wellbeing ====
Integrating food-producing trees and plants into urban landscapes enhances local self-sufficiency by increasing access to fresh, locally grown products. Still, as reported by the UN the actual and potential capacity for food production of urban agroforestry systems is often underestimated.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Oncini |first1=Filippo |last2=Hirth |first2=Steffen |last3=Mylan |first3=Josephine |last4=Robinson |first4=Clare H. |last5=Johnson |first5=David |date=2024-03-01 |title=Where the wild things are: How urban foraging and food forests can contribute to sustainable cities in the Global North |journal=Urban Forestry & Urban Greening |volume=93 |article-number=128216 |doi=10.1016/j.ufug.2024.128216 |bibcode=2024UFUG...9328216O |issn=1618-8667|doi-access=free}}</ref> Beyond the provision of food, these systems create green recreational spaces that support mental health, lower stress and improve community well-being.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wolf |first1=Kathleen L. |last2=Lam |first2=Sharon T. |last3=McKeen |first3=Jennifer K. |last4=Richardson |first4=Gregory R.A. |last5=van den Bosch |first5=Matilda |last6=Bardekjian |first6=Adrina C. |date=2020-06-18 |title=Urban Trees and Human Health: A Scoping Review |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |language=en |volume=17 |issue=12 |page=4371 |doi=10.3390/ijerph17124371 |doi-access=free |issn=1660-4601 |pmc=7345658 |pmid=32570770 |bibcode=2020IJERP..17.4371W}}</ref>

=== Examples/Projects ===

[[File:CapitaSpring2.jpg|thumb|upright|The food forest atop CapitaSpring in Singapore.]]

Urban [[Food Forest|food forests]] are a form of urban agroforestry that mimic the natural forest ecosystem. The practice combines trees with food production and can be implemented within cities and on rooftops.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Favor |first=K. |date=September 2023 |title=Urban Agroforestry Tipsheet: food forests and beyond |url=https://attra.ncat.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/urban-agroforestry-tipsheet2-1.pdf |website=attra.ncat.org |publisher=ATTRA}}</ref> Some examples of this practice can be found in [[Singapore]] where [[roof garden]]s are utilised for urban agroforestry.<ref>{{Cite web |title=From Rooftops to Plates: Singapore's Urban Farming for a Sustainable Future {{!}} Southeast Asia |url=https://th.boell.org/en/2025/08/25/rooftops-plates-singapores-urban-farming |access-date=2026-02-02 |publisher=Heinrich Böll Foundation}}</ref>

[[File:Pear orchard - geograph.org.uk - 239741.jpg|thumb|A pear orchard near Faversham]]

[[Community orchard]]s (a prominent form of [[Community gardening|community gardens]]) represent further examples of urban agroforestry, as fruit and/or nut trees are planted (often in linear patterns) and managed by a community.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lovell |first1=Sarah |last2=Hayman |first2=Jann |last3=Hemmelgarn |first3=Hannah |last4=Hunter |first4=Andrea |last5=Taylor |first5=John |date=2021-11-07 |title=Community Orchards for Food Sovereignty, Human Health, and Climate Resilience: Indigenous Roots and Contemporary Applications |journal=Forests |volume=12 |issue=11 |page=1533 |doi=10.3390/f12111533 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021Fore...12.1533L |issn=1999-4907}}</ref>

A city farm becomes a form of urban agroforestry when it intentionally integrates trees and perennial crops with other agricultural components in the urban landscape, thus creating a multifunctional system that produces food while also supporting ecological and community benefits.<ref name="kf"/>

== Forest gardening ==

[[File:Forestgarden2.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Robert Hart (horticulturist)|Robert Hart]]'s forest garden in [[Shropshire]]. ]]

Forest gardening is a low-maintenance, [[Sustainable gardening|sustainable]],<ref>{{cite book |title=Sustaining Forest Ecosystems |author=Klaus von Gadow |author2=Juan Gabriel Álvarez González |author3=Chunyu Zhang |author4=Timo Pukkala |author5=Xiuhai Zhao |page=13 |publisher=Springer Nature |year=2021 |isbn=978-3-030-58714-7 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eyc9EAAAQBAJ&dq=%22sustainable+forest+management+system%22+%22forest+gardening%22&pg=PA13}}</ref> plant-based food production and agroforestry system based on [[woodland]] [[ecosystem]]s, incorporating [[fruit]] and [[Nut (fruit)|nut]] [[tree]]s, [[shrubs]], [[herb]]s, [[vine]]s and [[perennial vegetable]]s which have [[ecological yield|yields]] directly useful to humans. Making use of [[companion planting]], these can be [[Intercropping|intermixed]] to grow in a succession of layers to build a woodland habitat.

Forest [[gardening]] is a [[prehistory|prehistoric]] method of securing food in [[tropical climate|tropical areas]]. In the 1980s, [[Robert Hart (horticulturist)|Robert Hart]] coined the term "forest gardening" after adapting the principles and applying them to [[Temperateness|temperate climates]].<ref name="Crawford 2010 18">{{Cite book |last=Crawford |first=Martin |title=Creating a Forest Garden: Working with Nature to Grow Edible Crops |publisher=Green Books |year=2010 |page=18 |isbn=978-1-900322-62-1 |ol=24327991M}}</ref> Forest gardens, or home gardens, are common in the tropics, using [[intercropping]] to cultivate [[tree]]s, [[agriculture|crops]], and [[livestock]] on the same land. In [[Kerala]] in [[south India]] as well as in [[northeastern India]], the home garden is the most common form of land use and is also found in [[Indonesia]]. One example combines [[coconut]], [[black pepper]], [[Cocoa bean|cocoa]] and [[pineapple]]. These gardens exemplify [[polyculture]], and conserve much crop [[genetic diversity]] and [[heirloom plant]]s that are not found in [[monocultures]]. Forest gardens have been loosely compared to the religious concept of the [[Garden of Eden]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Bell |first=Graham |title=The permaculture garden |date=2004 |publisher=Permanent Publications |others=Sarah Bunker |isbn=1-85623-027-9 |location=East Meon, Hampshire, U.K. |oclc=60454349}}</ref>

Forest [[garden]]s are probably the world's oldest form of land use and most resilient [[agroecosystem]].<ref name="Hart-1996a">{{Cite book |last=Hart |first=Robert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N01940btQAQC |title=Forest Gardening: Cultivating an Edible Landscape |publisher=Chelsea Green |year=1996 |isbn=978-1-60358-050-2 |edition=2nd |location=White River Junction, VT}}</ref>{{RP|124}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=McConnell |first=Douglas John |title=The forest farms of Kandy: and other gardens of complete design |date=2 March 2017 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-1-351-88963-6 |oclc=976441721 |quote=Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest form of land use and most resilient agroecosystem. Robert Hart adapted forest gardening for the United Kingdom's temperate climate during the 1980s.}}</ref> First Nation villages in [[Alaska]] with forest gardens filled with nuts, stone fruit, berries, and herbs, were noted by an archeologist from [[Smithsonian Institution|the Smithsonian]] in the 1930s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Coan |first=K.E.D. |date=2021-05-18 |title=Indigenous forest gardens remain productive and diverse for over a century |url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2021/05/indigenous-forest-gardens-remain-productive-and-diverse-for-over-a-century/ |access-date=2021-05-19 |website=Ars Technica}}</ref>

Forest gardens are still common in the [[tropics]] and known as Kandyan forest gardens in [[Sri Lanka]];<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jacob |first1=V. J. |last2=Alles |first2=W. S. |year=1987 |title=Kandyan gardens of Sri Lanka |journal=Agroforestry Systems |volume=5 |issue=2 |page=123 |doi=10.1007/BF00047517 |bibcode=1987AgrSy...5..123J |s2cid=40793796}}</ref> {{Lang|es|huertos familiares}}, family orchards in [[Mexico]];<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 2, 2004 |title=Inspector Gadget's green fingers and politics |first=Richard |last=Boyle |url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/books/inspector-gadgets-green-fingers-and-politics/182058.article |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120119041135/http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/story.asp?storyCode=182058&sectioncode=34 |archive-date=January 19, 2012 |website=Times Higher Education}}</ref> agroforests; or shrub gardens. They have been shown to be a significant source of income and food security for local populations.<ref>{{cite book |last=McConnell |first=Douglas John |title=The economic structure of Kandyan forest-garden farms |year=1973 |pages= }}</ref>

Robert Hart adapted forest gardening for the [[United Kingdom]]'s temperate climate during the 1980s.<ref name="Crawford 2010 18"/>

=== In temperate climates ===

[[File:Robert Hart (horticulturist).jpg|thumb|left|Robert Hart, forest gardening pioneer]]

Hart began farming at [[Wenlock Edge]] in [[Shropshire]] to provide a healthy and therapeutic environment for himself and his brother Lacon. Starting as relatively conventional [[Smallholding|smallholders]], Hart soon discovered that maintaining large annual vegetable beds, rearing livestock and taking care of an [[orchard]] were tasks beyond their strength. However, a small bed of perennial vegetables and herbs he planted was looking after itself with little intervention.<ref>{{cite web |last=Burnett |first=Graham |title=Seven Storeys of Abundance; A visit to Robert Hart's Forest Garden |url=http://www.spiralseed.co.uk/forestgarden/page2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111117034606/http://www.spiralseed.co.uk/forestgarden/page2.html |archive-date=2011-11-17}}</ref>

Following Hart's adoption of a [[raw veganism|raw vegan diet]] for health and personal reasons, he replaced his farm animals with plants. The three main products from a forest garden are fruit, nuts and [[Leaf vegetable|green leafy vegetables]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Whitefield |first=Patrick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3rd3e69BnC8C |title=How to Make a Forest Garden |year=2002 |isbn=978-1-85623-008-7 |page=5|publisher=Permanent Publications}}</ref> He created a model forest garden from a 0.12 acre (500 m<sup>2</sup>) orchard on his farm and intended naming his gardening method ''ecological horticulture'' or ''ecocultivation''.<ref name="Hart-1996a"/>{{RP|45}} Hart later dropped these terms once he became aware that ''agroforestry'' and ''forest gardens'' were already being used to describe similar systems in other parts of the world.<ref name="Hart-1996a"/>{{RP|28, 43}} He was inspired by the [[forest farming]] methods of [[Toyohiko Kagawa]] and James Sholto Douglas, and the productivity of the Keralan home gardens; as Hart explained, "From the agroforestry point of view, perhaps the world's most advanced country is the Indian state of Kerala, which boasts no fewer than three and a half million forest gardens ... As an example of the extraordinary intensity of cultivation of some forest gardens, one plot of only {{convert|0.12|ha|acre|abbr=off}} was found by a study group to have twenty-three young coconut palms, twelve cloves, fifty-six bananas, and forty-nine pineapples, with thirty pepper vines trained up its trees. In addition, the smallholder grew fodder for his [[house-cow]]."<ref name="Hart-1996a"/>{{RP|4-5}}

The [[Agroforestry Research Trust]], managed by [[Martin Crawford]], runs experimental forest gardening projects on a number of plots in [[Devon]], United Kingdom.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Agroforestry Research Trust |url=http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/trustinf.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111108011007/http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/trustinf.html |archive-date=2011-11-08}}</ref> Crawford describes a forest garden as a low-maintenance way of [[Sustainable agriculture|sustainably producing food]] and other household products.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Forest gardening |url=http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/forgndg.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130211233059/http://www.agroforestry.co.uk/forgndg.html |archive-date=2013-02-11 |access-date=13 Feb 2013 |publisher=Agroforestry Research Trust}}</ref>

Fern used the term ''woodland gardening'', rather than forest gardening, in his book ''Plants for a Future''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Woodland Gardening |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/PlantUses.aspx?id=19 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111128033102/http://pfaf.org/user/PlantUses.aspx?id=19 |archive-date=2011-11-28}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Plants for a Future - The book |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/cmspage.aspx?pageid=32 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111128105319/http://pfaf.org/user/cmspage.aspx?pageid=32 |archive-date=2011-11-28}}</ref>

[[El Pilar]] on the [[Belize]]–[[Guatemala]] border features a forest garden to demonstrate [[Agriculture in Mesoamerica|traditional Maya agricultural]] practices.<ref name="Ford">{{Cite journal |last=Ford |first=Anabel |date=May 2, 2009 |title=El Pilar Archaeological Reserve for Maya Flora and Fauna |url=http://www.guatemala-times.com/archeology/others/1081-el-pilar-archaeological-reserve-for-maya-flora-and-fauna-.html |url-status=live |journal=The Guatemala Times |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090505115733/http://www.guatemala-times.com/archeology/others/1081-el-pilar-archaeological-reserve-for-maya-flora-and-fauna-.html |archive-date=May 5, 2009 |access-date=2009-07-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ford |first=Anabel |date=December 15, 2010 |title=Legacy of the Ancient Maya: The Maya Forest Garden |url=http://popular-archaeology.com/issue/january-2011/article/the-legacy-of-el-pilar-the-maya-forest-garden |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120115154220/http://popular-archaeology.com/issue/january-2011/article/the-legacy-of-el-pilar-the-maya-forest-garden |archive-date=January 15, 2012 |publisher=Popular Archaeology}}</ref> A further one acre model forest garden, called Känan K'aax (meaning 'well-tended garden' in Mayan), is funded by the [[National Geographic Society]] and developed at Santa Familia Primary School in [[Cayo District|Cayo]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=National Geographic Society Funds Mayan Garden |url=http://www.ambergristoday.com/content/stories/2011/may/27/national-geographic-society-funds-mayan-garden |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111223101847/http://www.ambergristoday.com/content/stories/2011/may/27/national-geographic-society-funds-mayan-garden |archive-date=2011-12-23}}</ref>

In the United States, the largest known food forest on public land is believed to be the seven acre [[Beacon Food Forest]] in Seattle, Washington.<ref name="Crosscut">{{Cite news |last=Mellinger |first= Robert |date=16 February 2012 |title=Nation's Largest Food Forest takes root on Beacon Hill |work=Crosscut |url=http://crosscut.com/2012/02/16/agriculture/21892/Nation-s-largest-public-Food-Forest-takes-root-on-Beacon-Hill |access-date=14 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330165843/http://crosscut.com/2012/02/16/agriculture/21892/Nation-s-largest-public-Food-Forest-takes-root-on-Beacon-Hill/ |archive-date=30 March 2012}}</ref> The Boston Food Forest Coalition promotes local forest gardens.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bukowski |first1=Catherine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=44ViDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA83 |title=The Community Food Forest Handbook: How to Plan, Organize, & Nurture Edible Gathering Places |last2=Munsell |first2=John |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-60358-644-3 |pages=83–86 |publisher=Chelsea Green |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081024110544/http://www.montviewfarm.org/ |archive-date=2008-10-24 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=An Urban Food Forest: The Gift of Harvest|first = Cara |last = Brostrom |url=http://tellnewengland.com/foodforest |website=tell New England}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=He's on a mission to turn Boston into a collection of food forests |url=https://www.dotnews.com/2018/he-s-mission-turn-boston-collection-food-forests |website=Dorchester Reporter |date=16 August 2018 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=May 10, 2018 |title=Community engagement sprouts fresh ideas and nonprofit leadership |url= https://www.gmafoundations.com/nonprofit-leadership-development/ |website=GMA Foundations}}</ref>

In Canada, Richard Walker has been developing and maintaining food forests in [[British Columbia]] for over 30 years. He developed a three-acre food forest that at maturity provided raw materials for a plant nursery and herbal business as well as food for his family.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Richard Walker |url=http://www.permaculturebc.com/Permaculture-Instructor-British-Columbia-Richard-Walker |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110910135747/http://www.permaculturebc.com/Permaculture-Instructor-British-Columbia-Richard-Walker |archive-date=2011-09-10}}</ref> The Living Centre has developed various forest garden projects in [[Ontario]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Forest Gardening |url=http://www.thelivingcentre.com/cms/forest-gardening-home-page |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130526003055/http://www.thelivingcentre.com/cms/forest-gardening-home-page |archive-date=2013-05-26}}</ref>

Since 2014, Gisela Mir and Mark Biffen have been developing a small-scale edible forest garden in [[Cardedeu]] near [[Barcelona]], Spain, for experimentation and demonstration.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-01-22 |title=El verger de Phoenicurus, un bosc comestible mediterrani |url=https://phoenicurus-permacultura.org/2016/01/22/el-verger-de-phoenicurus-un-bosc-comestible-mediterrani/ |access-date=2021-04-22 |website=phoenicurus |language=ca}}</ref>

== Forest farming ==

Forest farming is the cultivation of high-value specialty [[crops]] under a [[forest canopy]] that is intentionally modified or maintained to provide shade levels and habitat that favor growth and enhance production levels. Forest farming encompasses a range of cultivated systems from introducing plants into the [[understory]] of a timber stand to modifying forest stands to enhance the [[marketability]] and sustainable production of existing plants.<ref>{{cite web |title=Forest Farming |url=https://woodpelletmakingmachine.com/forest-farming/ |access-date=2016-01-20 |website=Forest Farming}}</ref>

[[Non-timber forest product]]s are plants, parts of plants, fungi, and other biological materials harvested from within and on the edges of natural, manipulated, or disturbed forests.<ref>Chamberlain 2009</ref> Examples include ginseng, shiitake mushrooms, decorative ferns, and pine straw.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Vaughan |first=R. C. |author2=J. F. Munsell |author3=J. L. Chamberlain |title=Opportunities for Enhancing Nontimber Forest Products Management in the United States. |journal=Journal of Forestry |year=2013 |volume=111 |issue=1 |pages=26–33 |doi=10.5849/jof.10-106 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== History ===

[[File:KAGAWA Toyohiko young.JPG |thumb |right |[[Toyohiko Kagawa]], forest farming pioneer]]

Forest farming has long been practiced around the world, as people have relied on fruits, nuts, seeds, and foliage from trees and shrubs to feed themselves and their livestock.<ref name=":11">{{cite book |last=Douglas |first=J.S. |title=Forest farming: towards a solution to problems of world hunger and conservation |year=1984 |publisher=Intermediate Technology Publications |location=London |author2=R. A. de J. Hart}}</ref>

In 1929, J. Russell Smith, emeritus Professor of Economic Geography at Columbia University, published "Tree Crops – A Permanent Agriculture," which stated that crop-yielding trees could provide useful substitutes for cereals in animal feeding programs, as well as conserve environmental health.<ref name="Douglas 1984">Douglas 1984</ref> [[Toyohiko Kagawa]] read and was heavily influenced by Smith's publication and began experimental cultivation under trees in Japan during the 1930s.

Through forest farming, or three-dimensional forestry, Kagawa addressed problems of soil erosion by persuading many of Japan's upland farmers to plant fodder trees to conserve soil, supply food and feed animals. He combined extensive plantings of walnut trees, harvested the nuts and fed them to the pigs, then sold the pigs as a source of income. When the walnut trees matured, they were sold for timber and more trees were planted so that there was a continuous cycle of economic cropping that provided both short-term and long-term income to the small landowner.<ref name=":11" /> The success of these trials prompted similar research in other countries. World War II disrupted communication and slowed advances in forest farming.<ref name="Douglas 1984" /> In the mid-1950s research resumed in places such as southern Africa. Kagawa was also an inspiration to [[Robert Hart (horticulturist)|Robert Hart]], who pioneered forest gardening in temperate climates in the sixties in Shropshire, England.<ref name="Hart-1996a" />

Livestock was formerly often considered part of the forest farming system. Now animals are typically excluded and agroforestry systems that integrate trees, forages and livestock are referred to as [[silvopasture]]s.<ref name=":12">{{cite book |last=Garrett |first=H.E. |title=North American agroforestry: an integrated science and practice |year=2009 |publisher=American Society of Agronomy |location=Madison, Wisconsin |edition=2nd |pages=}}</ref> Because forest farming combines the [[ecological stability]] of natural forests with productive agriculture systems, it is considered to have great potential for regenerating soils, restoring ground water supplies, controlling floods and droughts, and cultivating marginal lands.<ref name=":12" />

===Methods===

Forest farming methods may include thinning of overstocked tree stands; integrated entries to accomplish thinning so that systemic shock is minimized; and interactive management to maintain a cross-section of healthy trees and shrubs of all ages and species. Physical [[ecological disturbance|disturbance]] to the surrounding area should be minimized.<ref>{{cite book |title=Training manual for applied agroforestry practices |year=2006 |publisher=University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry |location=[[Columbia, Missouri]] |pages=}}</ref>

=== Food Forest ===
Food forest is a permaculture practice where it prioritizes the growth of perennial species and various layers of plants to create an edible landscape. It is characterized as a perennial polyculture.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last1=Frey |first1=Darrell |title=The food forest handbook: design and manage a home-scale perennial polyculture garden |last2=Czolba |first2=Michelle |date=2017 |publisher=new society publishers |isbn=978-1-55092-622-4 |location=Canada}}</ref> The seven layers of a food forest are as follows: Canopy trees, understory trees, shrub layer, herbaceous plants, ground cover plants, vines and root zone (rhizosphere).<ref name=":4"/> Food Garden or Food Forest are not confined to a specific geographical region or continent and can be established in various environments.<ref name=":4"/>  Food Forest are adaptable in various scale but require access to land where plants can be rooted and integrated into the soil, a key process of regenerative agriculture.<ref name=":4"/> Food Forests are composed primarily of native perennials crops and require careful design and planning before established in the soil, as they represent long-term agriculture systems, along with a foundational understanding of ecological principles.<ref name=":4"/>

==== Indigenous history ====
Indigenous peoples have managed their land for millennia, by applying various agroecology techniques and principles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Armstrong |first1=Chelsey Geralda |last2=Miller |first2=Jesse |last3=McAlvay |first3=Alex |last4=Ritchie |first4=Patrick Morgan |last5=Lepofsky |first5=Dana |date=2021-04-22 |title=Ecology and Society: Historical Indigenous Land-Use Explains Plant Functional Trait Diversity |url=https://ecologyandsociety.org/vol26/iss2/art6/ |journal=Ecology and Society |language=en |volume=26 |issue=2 |doi=10.5751/ES-12322-260206 |issn=1708-3087}}</ref> The ''Milpa'' system, is a sustainable horticulture technic used by the Maya, who are the Indigenous people of what is now known as Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.<ref name=":4"/> This ancient agroecological practice involves intercropping crops such as maize, beans, squash, and chilis.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Benrey |first1=Betty |last2=Bustos-Segura |first2=Carlos |last3=Grof-Tisza |first3=Patrick |date=2024-11-01 |title=The mesoamerican milpa system: Traditional practices, sustainability, biodiversity, and pest control |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1049964424002020 |journal=Biological Control |volume=198 |article-number=105637 |doi=10.1016/j.biocontrol.2024.105637 |bibcode=2024BiolC.19805637B |issn=1049-9644}}</ref> Similarly, The Haudenosaunee, the Indigenous inhabitant that is now known as United States and Canada, used a technic, referred to as the three sisters, which requires three crops: corn, bean and squash.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Communications |title=Food And Hunting |url=https://www.haudenosauneeconfederacy.com/historical-life-as-a-haudenosaunee/food-and-hunting/ |access-date=2026-05-01 |website=Haudenosaunee Confederacy |language=en-US}}</ref> Both of these techniques requires that the crops help each other by providing nutrients to the soil, ground cover, pest control, and stability.<ref name=":5" /> For millennia, Indigenous communities, The Chumash, Yurok, Karuk, Hupa and Miwok tribes, in what is now known as California have practiced traditional agroecological methods, including controlled burning, to support ecosystem health and maintain soil fertility.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Cagle |first=Susie |date=2019-11-21 |title='Fire is medicine': the tribes burning California forests to save them |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2019/nov/21/wildfire-prescribed-burns-california-native-americans |access-date=2026-05-01 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

==== Contemporary context ====
In the 21st century, food forests have made a resurgence to address issues that current industrial agriculture practices poses.<ref name=":4" /> Agriculture contributes to nearly 30% of greenhouse gases.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=2016-04-13 |title=Greenhouse gas reduction |url=http://www.iaea.org/topics/greenhouse-gas-reduction |access-date=2026-05-01 |website=www.iaea.org |language=en}}</ref> Much of the emission is caused by monoculture techniques, where one single crop is grown in a field.<ref name=":6" /> With modern concern of food system, climate change and sustainable living, many experts have addressed permaculture as a mitigation tool.<ref name="Hathaway 239–250">{{Cite journal |last=Hathaway |first=Mark D. |date=2016-06-01 |title=Agroecology and permaculture: addressing key ecological problems by rethinking and redesigning agricultural systems |journal=Journal of Environmental Studies and Sciences |language=en |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=239–250 |doi=10.1007/s13412-015-0254-8 |bibcode=2016JEnSS...6..239H |issn=2190-6491}}</ref> Today, many Indigenous communities are reclaiming control over their food systems as a way of decolonization and resilience.<ref name="Lakhani">{{Cite news |last=Lakhani |first=Nina |date=2022-06-17 |title=The farmers restoring Hawaii's ancient food forests that once fed an island |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/jun/17/hawaii-traditional-farming-methods-ancient-food-forests |access-date=2026-05-01 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> In Hawaiʻi, traditional farmers are working to restore lands damaged by agrochemical corporations across the archipelago by revitalizing ancestral food forest systems that sustained their communities for millennia.<ref name="Lakhani"/>

Agroforestry (also known as agro-sylviculture or forest farming) is a land use management system that integrates trees with crops or pasture. It combines agricultural and forestry technologies. As a polyculture system, an agroforestry system can produce timber and wood products, fruits, nuts, other edible plant products, edible mushrooms, medicinal plants, ornamental plants, animals and animal products, and other products from both domesticated and wild species.
Agroforestry can be practiced for economic, environmental, and social benefits, and can be part of sustainable agriculture. Apart from production, benefits from agroforestry include improved farm productivity, healthier environments, reduction of risk for farmers, beauty and aesthetics, increased farm profits, reduced soil erosion, creating wildlife habitat, less pollution, managing animal waste, increased biodiversity, improved soil structure, and carbon sequestration.
Agroforestry practices are especially prevalent in the tropics, especially in subsistence smallholdings areas, with particular importance in sub-Saharan Africa. Due to its multiple benefits, for instance in nutrient cycle benefits and potential for mitigating droughts, it has been adopted in the US and Europe.
